questions.question: Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist and polar explorer, spoke to a meeting of geologists in Frankfurt in January 1912. He put before them a new idea about Earth's continents, which he later set out in a book. What did he claim about the continents?
questions.answer: They were once one land that broke up and drifted apart
choices: They were once one land that broke up and drifted apart
They have stood in the same places since Earth was young
They can rise and sink in place but never move sideways
Large parts of them sank long ago to form the ocean floors
questions.context: Wegener argued that all of today's continents had once been joined in a single supercontinent, which broke apart, its pieces drifting slowly to where they lie now. Most geologists of his day held that the continents and oceans had kept their places, rising or sinking at most, and many saw Wegener, a weather scientist, as an outsider to their field.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade plate tectonics opens with Wegener's 1912 proposal that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart.

questions.question: Alfred Wegener noticed something at the end of 1910 and wrote about it to the woman he would later marry. A year later he wrote to her father that his whole idea of moving continents had grown from it. What had he noticed?
questions.answer: The way two coasts across an ocean fit together
choices: The way two coasts across an ocean fit together
The same fossil reptile on two continents far apart
The same kind of rock in mountains across an ocean
Seams of coal in a land now buried under ice
questions.context: He asked whether the east coast of South America did not fit exactly against the west coast of Africa, as if the two had once been joined. Others had seen the fit before him, and Wegener learned of the matching fossils only in the autumn of 1911; then he hunted for more proof in rocks and fossils. He later called the lost supercontinent Pangaea, from Greek words meaning 'all the land'.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade texts tell how the jigsaw fit of South America and Africa set Wegener thinking that the continents had moved.

questions.question: Laid together along their shorelines, South America and Africa leave gaps and overlaps. Edward Bullard, a British geophysicist, matched them by computer in 1965 along a different line, and the fit came out snug. Where does that line lie?
questions.answer: Under the sea, at the edge of the continental shelf
choices: Under the sea, at the edge of the continental shelf
Under the sea, along the ridge in the middle of the ocean
On land, along the foot of the cliffs behind the beaches
On land, along the mountain ranges near each coast
questions.context: A continent does not end at its shore: its rock runs on under shallow sea as the continental shelf, and the shoreline is only where the sea happens to stand, which was about 120 metres lower in the ice ages. Bullard fitted the two continents along a line about 900 metres down, on the steep slope where the shelf gives way to the deep sea floor. The ridge in the middle of the ocean lies far out between them, where new sea floor is made.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-ESS2-3 names the shapes of the continents, including their continental shelves, among the evidence of past plate motion that seventh grade analyses.

questions.question: Alfred Wegener needed a force to move the continents, and he offered two: a push from Earth's spin, which he said flung them away from the poles, and the pull of the tides. Harold Jeffreys, a British geophysicist, worked out the size of those forces in 1924. What did he find?
questions.answer: They were far too weak to move a continent
choices: They were far too weak to move a continent
They were just strong enough to move a continent
They would move the continents faster than he said
They pushed the continents toward the poles, not away
questions.context: Jeffreys showed that a tide strong enough to shift a continent would stop Earth turning in less than a year, and Wegener could show no force strong enough. That was the fair heart of the case against drift, and Wegener admitted it: in 1929 he wrote that 'the Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.'
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that most geologists rejected drift because no known force could move the continents.

questions.question: Wegener's critics agreed that fossils of Mesosaurus, a small swimming reptile, lie in rocks of the same age in southern Africa and in South America, with an ocean between them. Most of them explained the find without moving any continents at all. How did they explain it?
questions.answer: A strip of land once joined the two, then sank
choices: A strip of land once joined the two, then sank
The reptiles swam across the ocean between them
Floating logs carried the reptiles over the sea
The same reptile arose on each land by itself
questions.context: Most geologists held that bridges of land had once linked the continents and later sank beneath the sea. Wegener answered that a bridge made of a continent's light rock could not sink into the denser rock of the sea floor and vanish, and plate tectonics later did away with the need for the bridges.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade accounts of Wegener set his drift against the sunken land bridges that most geologists of his day preferred.

questions.question: Marie Tharp, a geologist kept off research ships because she was a woman, drew maps of the Atlantic floor from depths that ships' echo sounders had measured. In 1952 she found a deep valley running down the crest of the ridge in mid-ocean. Bruce Heezen, who worked with her, said it looked too much like continental drift and waved it off as "girl talk". What changed his mind?
questions.answer: Undersea earthquakes turned out to line up along it
choices: Undersea earthquakes turned out to line up along it
A deep-diving submarine went down and saw it
Satellites photographed it from high above Earth
The head of their laboratory took her side
questions.context: Howard Foster had plotted the centres of undersea earthquakes for a project to lay cables across the ocean, and when his map was laid over Tharp's, the earthquakes ran along her valley, so the rift was active. Heezen came round in 1953, and their later maps showed a ridge running all the way round the globe.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade plate tectonics credits Marie Tharp's sea-floor maps and the rift down the mid-ocean ridge with reviving Wegener's idea.

questions.question: After the Second World War, ships towed magnetometers, instruments that measure magnetism, back and forth over the ocean. The rock of the sea floor turned out to be striped: long bands run beside the mid-ocean ridges, each band's magnetism unlike its neighbours'. What do the stripes record?
questions.answer: Times when Earth's magnetic field flipped
choices: Times when Earth's magnetic field flipped
Times when Earth's magnetic field weakened
Times when the seawater held more iron
Times when the Sun was more active
questions.context: Lava welling up at a ridge cools into rock, and as it cools, grains of an iron mineral line up with Earth's magnetic field and lock its direction in. Every so often the field flips, so that a compass needle would point south instead of north, and each flip starts a new stripe. A ship's magnetometer reads the bands as stronger and weaker, but what they record is the field's direction.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade texts teach the magnetic stripes in the sea floor as a record of flips in Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews, two British scientists, made a prediction in 1963. If new sea floor forms along a ridge and moves off on both sides, they said, the magnetic stripes in the sea-floor rock must lie in a telling pattern. A ship's readings across a ridge two years later showed that pattern almost perfectly. What was it?
questions.answer: Matching stripes on each side, in mirror image
choices: Matching stripes on each side, in mirror image
Stripes that differ from one side to the other
Stripes that grow wider farther from the ridge
Evenly spaced stripes, all of the same width
questions.context: Each side of the ridge carries away half of every stripe as it forms, so the two sides keep the same record, like a tape recorder with two heads, and on both sides wide and narrow stripes come mixed. Walter Pitman's 'magic profile', taken by the research ship Eltanin across a ridge in the far south of the Pacific, matched its own mirror image almost perfectly.
questions.grade_note: Middle-school texts teach that the stripes are mirror images on the two sides of a ridge, the evidence for sea-floor spreading.

questions.question: Plate tectonics, the theory that geologists accepted in the 1960s, grew out of Alfred Wegener's idea of drifting continents. Geologists today say that Wegener was right about most of his idea, but wrong about one major part of it. Which part did he get wrong?
questions.answer: That the continents plough through the sea floor
choices: That the continents plough through the sea floor
That the continents were once joined together
That continents are of lighter rock than the sea floor
That the continents are still moving today
questions.context: Wegener pictured each continent pushing through the ocean floor like an ice floe through the sea, and his critics rightly said the sea floor was far too firm for that, though he was right that continents are of lighter rock. Harry Hess proposed in the early 1960s that the sea floor itself spreads out from the mid-ocean ridges, carrying the continents along. Later in the 1960s this grew into plate tectonics: whole plates, continents and sea floor together, move.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade texts tell that Wegener was right that the continents move but wrong about how, since whole plates, sea floor and all, carry them.

questions.question: Alfred Wegener died on the Greenland ice in 1930, long before the argument over his idea was settled, and many geologists still doubted it in the 1950s. Yet by the end of the 1960s almost all geologists agreed that the continents move. What changed their minds?
questions.answer: Maps and magnetic readings of the sea floor
choices: Maps and magnetic readings of the sea floor
Satellite measurements of the continents moving
Proof that Earth is slowly swelling in size
Rocks that astronauts brought back from the Moon
questions.context: Maps of the ocean floor and its long ridges, and readings of the magnetism in its rock, gave geologists the evidence Wegener never had, and within a few years almost all of them changed their minds. Satellites first measured the continents moving only in the 1980s, and the first Moon rocks reached Earth in July 1969, after most geologists had come round. No measurement has found Earth swelling.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade closes the drift story with the sea-floor evidence that turned geologists round, the standard case of science changing with new evidence.

Fact-check (uncertain): 'could name no better force' was too strong, since his 1929 edition may have raised convection; now 'could show no force strong enough' (F35). Judge (medium, overlap) with plates-at-work d8c219c10d: that final keys mantle churning and only its context says spin and tides are too weak; the lead's ruling gives the missing force to this unit, and the judge offered accepting the overlap as one fix, so the key stays on Jeffreys's finding, which differs from anything plates-at-work keys.

dropped.question: Alfred Wegener's book of 1915 called his supercontinent the Urkontinent, German for the primal continent. In the 1920 edition he used a name made of two Greek words instead, and that is the name that stuck: Pangaea. What does Pangaea mean?
dropped.why: Judge drop (high, grade): it asked only what the name Pangaea means, which teaches nothing of the idea; 'pan-' (pandemic, panorama) gives 'all' away once the stem says the name is Greek; and the geography bank's T2 already keys the name and glosses it. Fact-check (uncertain): 'instead' and the 1920 date were shaky too. The name now lives in b89c654cb5's context, and the slot goes to the shelf fit.
